about: Dimensional Analysis is a short Michaelmas Term course in Part IA of the Cambridge Engineering Tripos: four lectures at the start of term, followed by two laboratory experiments that apply the ideas to model testing. In the 2025-26 syllabus it covers units and conversion, dimensional consistency, dimensionless groups and Buckingham's Pi theorem, dimensionless forms of governing equations, similarity and scale models, and using dimensional analysis to design experiments and present data. The laboratory work is coursework for standard credit, and the Part IA Guide notes that examination questions may also be set on the topic.
topics: Units: base and derived units, scales and conversion
Dimensionless groups and Buckingham's Pi theorem
Governing equations in dimensionless form and forms of relationships

notes.h: Units: base and derived units, scales and conversion
notes.body:
Every physical quantity is a number multiplied by a unit. Changing units changes the number but not the quantity. Getting this right is the first step in dimensional analysis and avoids costly engineering errors.

SI base units
- The SI has seven base units: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol) and candela (cd). Since 2019 they have been defined by fixing the values of physical constants.
- For mechanics problems, m, kg and s are enough. Heat transfer problems add K.

Derived units are products of powers of base units
- Force: newton, N = kg m s⁻².
- Pressure and stress: pascal, Pa = N m⁻² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻².
- Energy: joule, J = N m = kg m² s⁻².
- Power: watt, W = J s⁻¹ = kg m² s⁻³.
- Dynamic viscosity: Pa s = kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹.
- Prefixes scale by powers of ten, for example 1 MPa = 10⁶ Pa and 1 GPa = 10⁹ Pa. Steel has Young's modulus of roughly 200 GPa.

Other unit systems
- Engineers still meet imperial and US customary units, and some conversion factors are exact by definition:
  - 1 inch = 25.4 mm.
  - 1 foot = 0.3048 m.
  - 1 pound (mass) = 0.45359237 kg.
  - 1 mile = 1609.344 m, so 1 mph = 0.44704 m/s.
- Others follow from these: 1 lbf (pound-force) ≈ 4.448 N and 1 psi ≈ 6895 Pa.
- Temperature: T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15 and T(°F) = 1.8 T(°C) + 32. A temperature difference of 1 K equals 1 °C, which equals 1.8 °F. Keep temperature levels and temperature differences distinct.

How to convert reliably
- Multiply by a factor equal to one, for example (0.3048 m / 1 ft), so that the unwanted units cancel.
- Example: 60 mph = 60 × 0.44704 m/s ≈ 26.8 m/s.
- Example: 1 poise = 1 g cm⁻¹ s⁻¹ = 10⁻³ kg / (10⁻² m s) = 0.1 Pa s.

Empirical formulas with dimensional constants
- Some engineering formulas only work in particular units, because their constants carry hidden dimensions.
- Example: a formula v = 1.5√h is stated with v in ft/s and h in ft. Converting to SI, v(m/s) = 0.3048 × 1.5 √(h(m)/0.3048) = 1.5√0.3048 × √h ≈ 0.83√h.
- The constant changed because it really has dimensions of L^(1/2) T⁻¹. Here it plays the role of C√g.
- A formula written in dimensionless form has no such problem.

Exam tips: Carry units through every line of a calculation. Convert all data to one consistent system before substituting. Be suspicious of any formula whose numerical constants change when you change units: that is a sign that it is not written in dimensionless form.

The dimensions of a quantity show how it depends on the fundamental quantities mass M, length L, time T and temperature Θ, independently of the particular units. Square brackets denote 'dimensions of'.

Common dimensions to know
- Velocity [L T⁻¹]; acceleration [L T⁻²].
- Force [M L T⁻²]; energy and work [M L² T⁻²]; power [M L² T⁻³].
- Pressure, stress and Young's modulus [M L⁻¹ T⁻²].
- Density [M L⁻³].
- Dynamic viscosity μ [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹]; kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ [L² T⁻¹].
- Surface tension [M T⁻²].
- Second moment of area I [L⁴], so flexural rigidity EI has [M L³ T⁻²].
- Volume flow rate Q [L³ T⁻¹].
- Thermal conductivity k [M L T⁻³ Θ⁻¹]; thermal diffusivity α [L² T⁻¹]; heat transfer coefficient h [M T⁻³ Θ⁻¹]; specific heat capacity c [L² T⁻² Θ⁻¹].
- Angles, strains and ratios of like quantities are dimensionless.

Principle of dimensional homogeneity
- Every term in a physically valid equation must have the same dimensions. You can only add, subtract or equate like quantities.
- Example: Bernoulli's equation p + ½ρv² + ρgz = constant. Each term has dimensions [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]: ρv² gives (M L⁻³)(L² T⁻²) and ρgz gives (M L⁻³)(L T⁻²)(L).
- The arguments of exp, ln, sin, cos and so on must be dimensionless. So e^(−t/τ) requires τ to be a time, and sin ωt requires ω to have dimensions T⁻¹.

Uses of dimensional consistency
- Checking algebra: if a derived formula is not homogeneous, there is a mistake. Check at intermediate steps, not just at the end.
- Finding the dimensions of a constant. In Newton's law of gravitation F = Gm₁m₂/r², [G] = [F][r²]/[m²] = M⁻¹ L³ T⁻².
- Aiding memory: the period of a mass–spring oscillator must be built from m [M] and k [M T⁻²], so it is proportional to √(m/k). The only uncertainty is the numerical factor (2π).

Limitations
- A dimensionally consistent equation can still be wrong. Dimensional analysis cannot find dimensionless constants such as 2π or 1/3, or functions of dimensionless groups.
- Quantities with the same dimensions can be physically different. Torque and energy are both [M L² T⁻²].
- An empirical formula with dimensional constants may be inhomogeneous but still useful, provided the specified units are used.

Exam tips: Write the dimensions of every variable in a table before starting. When checking an equation, reduce each term to powers of M, L, T (and Θ) and compare them term by term.

notes.h: Dimensionless groups and Buckingham's Pi theorem
notes.body:
A dimensionless group is a product of powers of variables whose dimensions cancel completely. Its value is the same in every consistent system of units. Physical laws can always be written as relationships between such groups, because nature cannot depend on our arbitrary choice of units.

Buckingham's Pi theorem
- Suppose a physical relationship involves n variables, and these variables need k independent fundamental dimensions. Then the relationship can be rewritten as a relationship between n − k independent dimensionless groups Π₁, Π₂, …, Π_{n−k}.
- So f(q₁, …, qₙ) = 0 becomes F(Π₁, …, Π_{n−k}) = 0, or equivalently Π₁ = φ(Π₂, …, Π_{n−k}).
- Strictly, k is the rank of the dimensional matrix (the table of exponents of M, L, T, … for each variable). This is usually the number of dimensions that appear, but not always. For example, if M and T only ever appear together as M T⁻² in every variable of the problem, they count as one independent dimension and the rank is reduced.
- The groups are not unique. Any product of powers of groups is another valid group. What is fixed is how many independent groups there are.

Why it matters
- The number of things you need to vary in an experiment falls from n − 1 to n − k − 1.
- Example: the drag F on a sphere depends on ρ, U, D and μ. That is 5 variables and 3 dimensions, so there are 2 groups: F/(ρU²D²) = φ(ρUD/μ).
- A single curve of drag coefficient against Reynolds number replaces a four-dimensional table.

Famous dimensionless groups
- Reynolds number Re = ρUL/μ = UL/ν: inertia compared with viscous forces.
- Froude number Fr = U/√(gL): inertia compared with gravity. It matters for free-surface flows such as ships and weirs.
- Mach number Ma = U/a, where a is the speed of sound: compressibility.
- Drag coefficient C_D = F/(½ρU²A); pressure coefficient (p − p∞)/(½ρU²).
- Fourier number αt/L²: time compared with the time for heat to diffuse a distance L.
- Biot number hL/k_s: surface heat transfer compared with internal conduction in a solid of conductivity k_s.
- Strain, Poisson's ratio and angles are already dimensionless.

What the theorem does not tell you
- The form of the function φ. That must come from experiment or theory.
- Which variables are relevant. If you leave out an important variable, the analysis is wrong. If you include irrelevant ones, you get extra groups that experiments will show to have no effect.
- Numerical constants.

Special case: a single group
- If n − k = 1, the single group must be constant. Example: a simple pendulum at small amplitude depends on T, L and g (mass cannot appear, because no other variable contains M). One group, T√(g/L), must be a constant. Theory gives 2π.

Exam tips: Always state n, k and n − k explicitly, and show the dimensional matrix or table. Explain why each variable is included or excluded. That is where the engineering judgement lies, and it is where examiners award marks.

notes.h: Forming dimensionless relationships: the method of repeating variables
notes.body:
Method of repeating variables
- Step 1: list all n relevant variables, including the dependent variable, and write down their dimensions.
- Step 2: find k, the number of independent dimensions (the rank of the dimensional matrix).
- Step 3: choose k repeating variables. Together they must contain all k dimensions, and they must not be able to form a dimensionless group among themselves. Typically choose a density (mass), a velocity (time) and a length. Do not choose the dependent variable.
- Step 4: form each remaining variable into a group with powers of the repeating variables: Π = q × ρᵃ Uᵇ Dᶜ. Find a, b, c by equating the powers of each dimension to zero.
- Step 5: write Π₁ (containing the dependent variable) = φ(Π₂, …).

Worked example: drag on a sphere
- F = f(ρ, U, D, μ), with dimensions [M L T⁻²], [M L⁻³], [L T⁻¹], [L] and [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹].
- n = 5 and k = 3, so there are 2 groups. Repeating variables: ρ, U, D.
- For F: F ρᵃ Uᵇ Dᶜ. Mass: 1 + a = 0. Time: −2 − b = 0. Length: 1 − 3a + b + c = 0. So a = −1, b = −2, c = −2, giving Π₁ = F/(ρU²D²).
- For μ: similarly Π₂ = μ/(ρUD). Its reciprocal, Re = ρUD/μ, is the conventional choice.
- Result: F/(ρU²D²) = φ(Re).
- Check with a known limit: at very low Re, Stokes' law F = 3πμUD gives F/(ρU²D²) = 3π/Re. This is one particular form of φ.

Worked example: pressure drop in a pipe
- Δp over length ℓ of a pipe of diameter D, roughness ε, with flow speed U, density ρ and viscosity μ.
- n = 7 and k = 3, so there are 4 groups: Δp/(ρU²) = φ(ρUD/μ, ℓ/D, ε/D).
- Physical argument: in a long pipe with fully developed flow, Δp is proportional to ℓ. This gives (Δp/ℓ)D/(ρU²) = φ(Re, ε/D), the basis of the Darcy friction factor charts.

Worked example: blast wave (G. I. Taylor)
- The radius R of a strong blast wave depends on the energy released E, the time t and the air density ρ. Ambient pressure is negligible for a very strong shock.
- n = 4 and k = 3, so there is one group: R(ρ/(Et²))^(1/5) = constant.
- So R ∝ E^(1/5) t^(2/5) ρ^(−1/5). Photographs of R against t can therefore be used to estimate E.

Practical points
- Choose groups with physical meaning (Re, Fr, C_D) rather than any algebraically valid set.
- A ratio of two lengths, or of two quantities with the same dimensions, is a group immediately and needs no algebra.
- If an independent variable cannot be combined with any others, it probably should not be in the list. For example, mass in the pendulum problem cannot form a group, so the period cannot depend on it.
- Always check each final group by substituting the dimensions.

Exam tips: Set out the exponent equations neatly (one for each of M, L, T). Present the final relationship in the form 'dependent group = function of independent groups'. State any physical assumptions you used to reduce the number of groups, such as linearity or negligible viscosity.

notes.h: Governing equations in dimensionless form, and forms of dimensionless relationships
notes.body:
When the governing equation is known, writing it in dimensionless variables shows exactly which groups control the problem, often more clearly than the repeating-variable method.

Procedure
- Choose a characteristic scale for each variable: a length L, a time scale τ, a displacement X₀, a temperature difference ΔT₀, and so on.
- Define dimensionless variables, for example x̃ = x/X₀ and t̃ = t/τ.
- Substitute and divide through so that one term has coefficient 1. The remaining coefficients are the dimensionless groups.

Example: the damped oscillator
- m ẍ + c ẋ + kx = 0 with x(0) = X₀ and ẋ(0) = 0.
- Choose τ = √(m/k) and x̃ = x/X₀. The equation becomes x̃″ + 2ζ x̃′ + x̃ = 0, where ζ = c/(2√(mk)) and the primes denote d/dt̃.
- So x/X₀ = φ(t√(k/m), ζ). This has 3 groups from 6 variables (x, t, m, c, k, X₀) and 3 dimensions, as the Pi theorem predicts. Here the equation also identifies which combination of groups is natural.

Example: transient heat conduction
- ∂T/∂t = α ∂²T/∂x² in a slab of thickness L.
- With x̃ = x/L and t̃ = αt/L², the equation becomes ∂θ/∂t̃ = ∂²θ/∂x̃², where θ is a dimensionless temperature such as (T − T₀)/ΔT₀.
- The solution depends on time only through the Fourier number αt/L². A geometrically similar body half the size, made of the same material, reaches the same dimensionless state in a quarter of the time.
- If heat is lost at the surface, the boundary condition brings in the Biot number hL/k_s.

Example: fluid flow
- Non-dimensionalising the equations of viscous flow brings in the Reynolds number as the only parameter (for incompressible flow without a free surface). This is why Re dominates fluid mechanics.

Forms of dimensionless relationships
- General form: Π₁ = φ(Π₂, Π₃, …). The function must be found by experiment or theory.
- One group only: Π₁ = constant. Examples are the pendulum and the blast wave.
- Physical constraints can fix the form. For example, linear elasticity means beam deflection δ is proportional to load P. Since δ/L = φ(PL²/EI), φ must be linear, so δ = C PL³/EI. Beam theory gives C = 1/3 for a cantilever with an end load and C = 1/48 for a simply supported beam with a central load.
- Power laws: experiments often show Π₁ ≈ C Π₂ᵃ over a range. A straight line on log–log axes has slope a.
- Limiting regimes: if one group is very large or very small, its effect may disappear. For example, the drag coefficient of a bluff body is roughly independent of Re over a wide range of high Re, because viscosity then matters little, except in thin boundary layers and at the transition to turbulence.

Exam tips: When non-dimensionalising, state your scales and why you chose them. The best scales make the dimensionless variables of order one. Say explicitly which groups remain and what they mean physically. Use known exact solutions to identify constants that dimensional analysis alone cannot give.

Model testing lets engineers predict the behaviour of a large, expensive or dangerous prototype from measurements on a smaller model. Dimensional analysis tells you how to run the test and how to scale the results.

Types of similarity
- Geometric similarity: the model is an exact scale copy. All length ratios are equal, including roughness, if it matters.
- Kinematic similarity: velocity ratios (flow patterns) are the same at corresponding points.
- Dynamic similarity: the ratios of all forces are the same. This is achieved when every independent dimensionless group has the same value in the model as in the prototype.

The principle
- If Π₁ = φ(Π₂, Π₃, …) and the model matches every independent group (Π₂, Π₃, …), then Π₁ must also match. So you measure Π₁ on the model and convert to the prototype.

Example: Reynolds similarity
- A 1/10-scale model in the same fluid needs U_m D_m = U_p D_p, so U_m = 10U_p. This is often impractical.
- For a car tested at 1/4 scale in air, matching a 30 m/s prototype needs 120 m/s. At that speed compressibility (Mach number) starts to matter, which spoils the similarity.
- Solutions: change the fluid (for example, use water, whose kinematic viscosity is about 15 times smaller than that of air), pressurise the tunnel, or rely on the drag coefficient being roughly independent of Re at high Re.

Example: Froude similarity (ships and weirs)
- Wave-making depends on Fr = U/√(gL). Since g is the same for model and prototype, U_m/U_p = √(L_m/L_p).
- A 100 m ship at 10 m/s, modelled at 1:25 (4 m), needs U_m = 10/√25 = 2 m/s.
- At equal Fr and equal density, forces scale as ρU²L², i.e. as L³. So the prototype force is 25³ = 15,625 times the model force.

Incomplete similarity
- You cannot generally match both Fr and Re with the same fluid. Froude matching requires U ∝ √L, but Reynolds matching requires U ∝ 1/L.
- In ship testing the standard approach is to match Fr and correct separately for skin friction, which depends mainly on Re. Engineers must judge which groups matter most.
- Distortion: in river models the vertical scale is often exaggerated so that the depths are not unrealistically small. Results then need careful interpretation.

Scaling structural models
- For an elastic structure loaded by a force P, similarity requires P/(EL²) to be the same, along with Poisson's ratio and the geometry.
- A model made from a different material, or at a different scale, must have its load scaled accordingly. Deflections then scale with length.
- If self-weight matters, ρgL/E must also match, which is hard to achieve at small scale.

Exam tips: List the groups, decide which must be matched, and write the scaling law for each quantity (speed, force, power, time) as a ratio. State the assumptions, such as the same fluid, the same g, or a negligible effect of Re. Discuss which similarity requirements cannot be met and the consequences.

notes.h: Designing experiments, presenting data and the Part IA experiments (illustrative)
notes.body:
Dimensional analysis is one of the most practical tools in experimental engineering. It tells you what to vary, how to plot the results, and how to generalise from a single rig.

Designing an experiment
- List the variables and form the groups. Then plan to vary each independent group in turn, rather than each dimensional variable.
- Fewer runs are needed, and you can choose whichever dimensional variable is easiest to change. To vary Re, for example, you might change the speed rather than the viscosity.
- To test whether a variable matters, vary its group while holding the others fixed. If the dependent group does not change, the variable can be dropped.
- Range: make sure the experiment covers the range of groups that applies to the real application. Results outside the tested range of Re or Fr may not extrapolate.

Presenting data
- Plot the dependent group against the independent group, for example C_D against Re.
- Data from different sizes, speeds and fluids should then collapse onto a single curve. If they do not, a relevant variable has been missed, or there is experimental error.
- Use log–log axes when a power law is expected. The slope gives the exponent, and the intercept gives the constant.
- Show uncertainty, and keep the scaling consistent between data sets.

The kinds of experiment met in Part IA
The 2025-26 syllabus lists laboratory work applying dimensional analysis to model testing. The experiments involve the deflection of an elastic beam, the temperature variation of two blocks starting at different temperatures, and flow over a V-notch weir. The outlines below are illustrative: they show how dimensional analysis applies to each problem, but they are not taken from the laboratory handout, whose variables, procedure and plots may differ. Follow the handout in the lab.

Elastic beam
- δ depends on P, L, E and I. Since P and E share the combination M T⁻², the dimensional matrix has rank 2, so there are 3 groups: δ/L, P/(EL²) and I/L⁴.
- Beam theory says only the product EI matters, which combines the last two groups into PL²/(EI).
- Linearity then gives δEI/(PL³) = constant. Plotting δ against PL³/(EI) for different beams should give a single straight line through the origin.

Flow over a V-notch weir
- If viscosity and surface tension are negligible, Q depends on g, the head H and the notch angle θ.
- The groups give Q/(g^(1/2) H^(5/2)) = φ(θ). For a fixed notch, Q ∝ H^(5/2), so a log–log plot of Q against H should have slope 5/2.
- Doubling the flow raises the head by a factor of 2^(2/5) ≈ 1.32. Departures at small heads indicate that the neglected effects (viscosity, surface tension) are becoming important.

Two blocks at different temperatures
- The temperature history depends on the block size L, the thermal diffusivity α, the conductivities and the initial temperature difference.
- Plotting a dimensionless temperature against the Fourier number αt/L² should collapse the results for different sizes. For blocks of the same materials, and if no other group (such as a Biot number for the contact) changes, a block of half the size reaches the same state in a quarter of the time.

Exam tips: Explain how you would plot your data to test a dimensional prediction, and what result would confirm or refute it. Questions may also ask you to criticise an experimental plan, for example one that varies only a single dimensional variable, or that cannot achieve the full-scale value of a key group.

questions.q: Approximately what is 60 mph in m/s?
questions.why: 1 mph = 0.44704 m/s, so 60 mph = 26.8 m/s. 96.6 is the value in km/h, not m/s. 16.7 is 60 km/h converted to m/s, which treats the miles as kilometres. 18.3 m/s uses the foot factor, treating 60 mph as if it were 60 ft/s (60 × 0.3048).

questions.q: An empirical formula v = 1.5√h holds with v in ft/s and h in ft. What is the constant when v is in m/s and h is in m?
questions.why: v(m/s) = 0.3048 × 1.5 √(h/0.3048) = 1.5√0.3048 × √h ≈ 0.83√h. The constant has dimensions L^(1/2) T⁻¹, so it changes with the units and cannot stay at 1.5. 2.7 comes from dividing by √0.3048 instead of multiplying. 0.46 multiplies by 0.3048 but forgets the change in h.

questions.q: Express 1 psi (pound-force per square inch) in pascals, given 1 lbf ≈ 4.448 N and 1 inch = 25.4 mm exactly. Show your working with unit factors.
markScheme: ≈ 6.89 × 10³ Pa (about 6.9 kPa)
Uses unit factors so that the units cancel visibly
questions.modelAnswer: 1 psi = 1 lbf/in² × (4.448 N/1 lbf) × (1 in/0.0254 m)². Now (0.0254)² = 6.4516 × 10⁻⁴, so 1 psi = 4.448/(6.4516 × 10⁻⁴) N/m² ≈ 6894 Pa ≈ 6.9 kPa. As a check, atmospheric pressure is about 101 kPa, which is close to the familiar 14.7 psi.

questions.q: What are the dimensions of dynamic viscosity μ (defined by shear stress = μ × velocity gradient)?
questions.why: Stress [M L⁻¹ T⁻²] divided by velocity gradient [T⁻¹] gives [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹]. L² T⁻¹ is kinematic viscosity μ/ρ. M L⁻¹ T⁻² is stress itself. M L T⁻¹ is momentum.

questions.q: Which equation is dimensionally inconsistent? (ρ density, v speed, p pressure, g gravitational acceleration, h height, m mass, k spring stiffness, x displacement, E energy)
questions.why: ½ρv has dimensions (M L⁻³)(L T⁻¹) = M L⁻² T⁻¹, not those of pressure (M L⁻¹ T⁻²), so that equation is inconsistent. In the version with ½ρv², every term has the dimensions of pressure. In the two energy equations, every term has dimensions M L² T⁻², since k has dimensions M T⁻².

questions.q: A student claims that the deflection of a cantilever is δ = PL²/(3EI), where P is the end load, L the length, E Young's modulus and I the second moment of area. Use dimensions to show that this must be wrong, and suggest the correct power of L.
markScheme: [P] = M L T⁻², [E] = M L⁻¹ T⁻², [I] = L⁴
[EI] = M L³ T⁻²
[PL²/(EI)] = (M L³ T⁻²)/(M L³ T⁻²) = dimensionless, but δ is a length
So the formula is inhomogeneous; need PLⁿ/(EI) with dimensions L, so n = 3
δ = PL³/(3EI) (the constant 1/3 cannot come from dimensions)
questions.modelAnswer: [P] = M L T⁻², [E] = M L⁻¹ T⁻² and [I] = L⁴, so [EI] = M L³ T⁻². Then [PL²/(EI)] = M L³ T⁻²/(M L³ T⁻²), which is dimensionless, but δ is a length. The formula is therefore dimensionally inconsistent and must be wrong. For PLⁿ/(EI) to be a length we need n − 2 = 1, so n = 3. The correct result from beam theory is δ = PL³/(3EI). Dimensional analysis fixes the power of L, but it cannot supply the factor 1/3.

questions.q: A problem involves 6 variables, which together involve the 3 dimensions M, L and T, and the dimensional matrix has rank 3. How many independent dimensionless groups are there?
questions.why: Buckingham's Pi theorem gives n − k = 6 − 3 = 3 groups. 6 is the number of variables. 2 would apply if the rank were 4, which is impossible with three dimensions. 9 adds instead of subtracting.

questions.q: The period T of a small-amplitude simple pendulum may depend on its length L, the bob mass m and g. What does dimensional analysis give?
questions.why: Mass is the only variable involving M, so it cannot appear in any group. With T, L and g there are 3 variables and 2 dimensions, giving 1 group, T√(g/L), which must be constant (2π in fact). φ(m) is impossible because m cannot be made dimensionless. √(mL/g) does not have dimensions of time. L/g has dimensions T², not T.

questions.q: State Buckingham's Pi theorem. Explain what the theorem does not tell you, and why choosing the list of variables is the critical step.
markScheme: n variables, k independent dimensions (rank of the dimensional matrix): the relationship reduces to one between n − k independent dimensionless groups
Groups are not unique; any products or powers of groups are also valid
It does not give the form of the function or the numerical constants
Missing a relevant variable gives a wrong result; including irrelevant variables adds spurious groups
So engineering judgement or experiment is needed to choose the variables
questions.modelAnswer: If a physical relationship involves n variables whose dimensions need k independent fundamental dimensions (strictly, the rank of the dimensional matrix), it can be written as a relationship between n − k independent dimensionless groups, Π₁ = φ(Π₂, …, Π_{n−k}). The groups are not unique, since any product of powers of groups is also a group. The theorem says nothing about the form of φ or about numerical constants, which must come from experiment or theory. The result is only as good as the list of variables. If a relevant variable is omitted (for example viscosity in low-speed flow), the predicted relationship is wrong. If irrelevant variables are included, the extra groups waste experimental effort until they are shown to have no effect. Choosing the variables therefore requires physical understanding of the problem.

questions.q: The drag F on a sphere depends on ρ, U, D and μ. Which is a correct dimensionless form?
questions.why: F/(ρU²D²) is dimensionless, and so is the Reynolds number ρUD/μ, giving the 5 − 3 = 2 groups. F/(ρUD) has dimensions L² T⁻¹, so it is not a group. F/(μUD²) has dimensions L⁻¹. The Froude number needs g, which is not in the variable list.

questions.q: The radius R of a strong blast wave depends only on the energy E, the time t and the air density ρ. How does R depend on t?
questions.why: Requiring R = C Eᵃ tᵇ ρᶜ to have dimensions of length gives a = 1/5, b = 2/5 and c = −1/5, so R ∝ (Et²/ρ)^(1/5). t^(1/2) is diffusive scaling. Linear growth would mean a constant speed. t^(1/5) confuses the exponent of t with that of E.

questions.q: The pressure drop Δp along a length ℓ of a smooth pipe of diameter D depends on the mean velocity U, the fluid density ρ and the viscosity μ. Use the method of repeating variables to find the dimensionless groups. Then use the physical fact that Δp ∝ ℓ in a long pipe to simplify the result.
markScheme: n = 6 (Δp, ℓ, D, U, ρ, μ), k = 3, so 3 groups
Repeating variables ρ, U, D
Groups Δp/(ρU²), ℓ/D and ρUD/μ (Re)
Δp/(ρU²) = φ(ℓ/D, Re)
Δp ∝ ℓ, so (Δp/ℓ)D/(ρU²) = ψ(Re), a friction factor depending only on Re
questions.modelAnswer: The variables are Δp [M L⁻¹ T⁻²], ℓ [L], D [L], U [L T⁻¹], ρ [M L⁻³] and μ [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹]. So n = 6 and k = 3, giving 3 groups. Take ρ, U and D as repeating variables. For Δp ρᵃ Uᵇ Dᶜ: from M, a = −1; from T, b = −2; from L, c = 0. So Π₁ = Δp/(ρU²). The ratio of lengths gives Π₂ = ℓ/D. Viscosity gives Π₃ = μ/(ρUD), or its reciprocal Re = ρUD/μ. So Δp/(ρU²) = φ(ℓ/D, Re). In a long pipe with fully developed flow, Δp is proportional to ℓ, so φ must be (ℓ/D) × ψ(Re). That gives (Δp/ℓ)D/(ρU²) = ψ(Re): a friction factor that depends only on the Reynolds number for a smooth pipe.

questions.q: Writing m ẍ + c ẋ + kx = 0 with t̃ = t√(k/m) leaves which single dimensionless parameter?
questions.why: Dividing through by k and using d/dt = √(k/m) d/dt̃ gives x″ + (c/√(mk))x′ + x = 0, so the parameter is the damping ratio ζ = c/(2√(mk)). c/k has dimensions of time. c/m has dimensions T⁻¹. √(k/m) is the natural frequency, which is dimensional and has been absorbed into t̃.

questions.q: Two geometrically similar blocks of the same material are cooled by conduction under similar conditions. The second is three times the size of the first. How long does it take to reach the same dimensionless temperature state?
questions.why: The dimensionless state depends on time through the Fourier number αt/L². With α the same, t ∝ L², so tripling the size multiplies the time by 9. A factor of 3 would be linear scaling, which conduction does not follow. 'The same time' ignores the size. √3 confuses the scaling the other way round: it is the diffusion distance that grows like √t, so time grows like L², not like √L.

questions.q: Linear elastic beam theory says the deflection δ of a beam under a point load P depends on P, L and EI. Use dimensional analysis together with linearity to find the form of the relationship. Explain why the constant differs between a cantilever and a simply supported beam.
markScheme: Variables δ [L], P [M L T⁻²], L [L], EI [M L³ T⁻²]
P and EI involve M and T only as M T⁻², so the rank is 2: 4 − 2 = 2 groups
δ/L = φ(PL²/EI)
Linearity (δ ∝ P) forces φ to be linear: δ = C PL³/EI
C depends on the support conditions and load position (1/3 for an end-loaded cantilever, 1/48 for a centrally loaded simply supported beam), which dimensional analysis cannot give
questions.modelAnswer: The variables are δ [L], P [M L T⁻²], L [L] and EI [M L³ T⁻²]. P and EI contain M and T only in the combination M T⁻², so the dimensional matrix has rank 2 and there are 4 − 2 = 2 groups: δ/L and PL²/(EI). So δ/L = φ(PL²/EI). For a linear elastic beam with small deflections, δ is proportional to P, so φ must be linear: δ/L = C PL²/(EI), i.e. δ = C PL³/(EI). C depends on the support and loading configuration, which is a dimensionless 'shape' of the problem. Beam theory gives C = 1/3 for a cantilever with an end load and C = 1/48 for a simply supported beam loaded at mid-span. Dimensional analysis alone cannot find these constants.

questions.q: A 1:25 scale model of a ship is tested in a towing tank to match the Froude number. If the ship travels at 10 m/s, what speed should the model be towed at?
questions.why: Equal Fr = U/√(gL) with the same g gives U_m = U_p√(L_m/L_p) = 10/5 = 2 m/s. 0.4 m/s scales the speed linearly with length. 10 m/s ignores scaling altogether. 250 m/s is Reynolds scaling (U ∝ 1/L), which is impractical and is not the criterion for wave-making.

questions.q: For the Froude-scaled ship model above (1:25, same water density), how does the prototype wave-making force compare with the force measured on the model?
questions.why: Force scales as ρU²L². With U² ∝ L, this is ∝ L³, so the ratio is 25³ = 15,625. 625 = 25² assumes equal speeds. 25 is linear scaling. 125 = 25^(3/2) is the speed ratio multiplied by the length ratio, which has no physical basis here.

questions.q: Explain the terms geometric, kinematic and dynamic similarity. Using the example of a ship model in a towing tank, explain why complete dynamic similarity is usually impossible and how engineers deal with this.
markScheme: Geometric: an exact scale copy, with all length ratios equal
Kinematic: the same velocity ratios and flow patterns at corresponding points
Dynamic: all force ratios equal, i.e. all independent dimensionless groups matched
Ship: wave-making needs equal Fr (U ∝ √L), friction needs equal Re (U ∝ 1/L in the same fluid), so both cannot be met
Match Fr, and estimate the frictional resistance separately (from Re-dependent friction data) for model and ship, correcting the result
questions.modelAnswer: Geometric similarity means the model is an exact scale copy of the prototype, with every length ratio equal. Kinematic similarity means velocities at corresponding points are in the same ratio, so the flow patterns look alike. Dynamic similarity means all force ratios are the same, which is achieved when every independent dimensionless group has the same value in the model and the prototype. For a ship, wave-making resistance depends on the Froude number U/√(gL), and skin friction depends on the Reynolds number UL/ν. With water in both cases, matching Fr requires U ∝ √L, while matching Re requires U ∝ 1/L. A small model cannot satisfy both. The usual practice is to match Fr, so that the wave pattern is correctly scaled, measure the total resistance, subtract an estimate of the model's frictional resistance (from friction data at the model Re), scale the remaining wave resistance by Froude scaling, and add the full-scale frictional resistance estimated at the ship's Re.

questions.q: For a V-notch weir with negligible viscous and surface-tension effects, how should log Q plotted against log H look for a fixed notch?
options: A curve whose shape depends on the notch angle
questions.why: Dimensional analysis gives Q/(g^(1/2)H^(5/2)) = φ(θ). For a fixed θ, Q ∝ H^(5/2), which is a straight line of slope 5/2 on log–log axes. Slope 3/2 is the result for a rectangular weir, whose width is an extra fixed length. 1/2 is the power of g, not of H. The angle changes only the intercept, not the shape.

questions.q: Drag measurements from three different spheres in two different fluids are plotted as C_D against Re, and they do not fall on a single curve. What is the most likely conclusion?
options: A relevant variable has been left out of the analysis (or there are significant experimental errors)
The Pi theorem does not apply to drag
Re should be plotted on a linear scale
questions.why: If the variable list were complete, all the data would collapse onto C_D = φ(Re). Scatter between data sets points to a missing group, such as surface roughness, Mach number or wall effects, or to errors. The Pi theorem always applies. The choice of axis scale cannot change whether the data collapse. Size alone is already accounted for through Re.

questions.q: You are asked to find how the flow rate Q over a V-notch weir depends on the head H. Explain how dimensional analysis guides the design of the experiment and the presentation of the results. State the expected relationship, and how you would recognise when the simple analysis breaks down.
markScheme: Variables Q, g, H, θ (neglecting μ, surface tension): 4 variables, 2 dimensions, 2 groups
Q/(g^(1/2)H^(5/2)) = φ(θ); for a fixed notch Q ∝ H^(5/2)
Experiment: measure Q over a range of H; plot log Q against log H (or Q/H^(5/2) against H)
Expect slope 5/2 (or a constant Q/H^(5/2)); the intercept gives the discharge constant for that θ
Deviations at small H show that viscosity and surface tension (Re and Weber number) matter; the result should not be extrapolated outside the tested range
questions.modelAnswer: If viscosity and surface tension are neglected, Q depends on g, H and the notch angle θ. With 4 variables and 2 dimensions (L and T), there are 2 groups: Q/(g^(1/2)H^(5/2)) and θ. So Q = g^(1/2)H^(5/2)φ(θ), and for a given notch Q ∝ H^(5/2). This tells you that only H needs to be varied for a fixed notch, and that you do not need to vary g. Measure Q over as wide a range of H as possible and plot log Q against log H. A straight line of slope 5/2 confirms the analysis, and the intercept gives the discharge constant for that angle. Alternatively, plot Q/H^(5/2) against H, which should be constant. At small heads, the data will depart from the line because viscous and surface-tension effects (Reynolds and Weber numbers) become important. These are the groups that were neglected, so the relationship should be used only within the range that was tested.

questions.q:
Water (density 1000 kg/m³, kinematic viscosity 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s) flows at 2 m/s through a smooth pipe of diameter 0.1 m. An engineer proposes to predict the pressure gradient by testing air (density 1.2 kg/m³, kinematic viscosity 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s) in a geometrically similar smooth pipe of diameter 0.05 m.
(a) Using dimensional analysis, show that the pressure gradient in a long pipe satisfies (Δp/ℓ)D/(ρU²) = ψ(UD/ν). State the assumptions. [6]
(b) Find the air speed needed for dynamic similarity. [4]
(c) At this speed the air test gives a pressure gradient of 650 Pa/m. Predict the pressure gradient in the water pipe. [6]
(d) Comment on any limitation of the air test at this speed. [4]
markScheme: (a) Variables Δp, ℓ, D, U, ρ, μ (smooth pipe, incompressible, fully developed flow); 6 − 3 = 3 groups
(a) Δp/(ρU²) = φ(ℓ/D, Re); Δp ∝ ℓ in a long pipe gives (Δp/ℓ)D/(ρU²) = ψ(Re) with Re = UD/ν
(c) Equal ψ, so (Δp/ℓ)_w = (Δp/ℓ)_a × (ρU²/D)_w/(ρU²/D)_a
(c) (ρU²/D)_w = 40,000 and (ρU²/D)_a = 86,400, giving ≈ 301 Pa/m
(d) Mach number about 60/340 ≈ 0.18: compressibility is small but not entirely negligible; a long air pipe has significant density change if Δp is large; roughness must also be scaled
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For fully developed, incompressible flow in a smooth pipe, Δp depends on ℓ, D, U, ρ and μ. These 6 variables involve M, L and T, so there are 3 groups. Using ρ, U and D as repeating variables gives Δp/(ρU²), ℓ/D and Re = ρUD/μ = UD/ν, so Δp/(ρU²) = φ(ℓ/D, Re). In a long pipe, away from entry effects, the pressure falls linearly with distance, so Δp ∝ ℓ and φ = (ℓ/D)ψ(Re). Therefore (Δp/ℓ)D/(ρU²) = ψ(UD/ν). The assumptions are a smooth pipe (otherwise ε/D is another group), negligible compressibility, steady fully developed flow and geometric similarity.

(b) Re_water = UD/ν = 2 × 0.1/(1.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 2 × 10⁵. For similarity, the air must have the same Re: U_air = Re × ν_air/D_air = 2 × 10⁵ × 1.5 × 10⁻⁵/0.05 = 60 m/s.

(c) With equal Re, ψ is the same, so (Δp/ℓ) × D/(ρU²) is the same in both tests. Hence (Δp/ℓ)_water = (Δp/ℓ)_air × [ρU²/D]_water/[ρU²/D]_air. Here [ρU²/D]_water = 1000 × 4/0.1 = 40,000 and [ρU²/D]_air = 1.2 × 3600/0.05 = 86,400 (both in Pa/m). So (Δp/ℓ)_water = 650 × 40,000/86,400 ≈ 301 Pa/m.

(d) At 60 m/s the Mach number is about 60/340 ≈ 0.18. Density changes are roughly ½Ma², around 1–2%, so compressibility is small but not zero. The analysis assumed it was negligible, which is reasonable here but would fail at higher speeds. Over a long test pipe, the pressure drop (about 0.65 kPa per metre) also changes the air density along the pipe, so the gradient should be measured over a modest length. Any wall roughness must be scaled geometrically, otherwise ε/D differs between the tests. High air speeds also need a powerful fan and produce noise. Despite these points, the test is a sound application of Reynolds similarity.

questions.q:
The tip deflection δ of a cantilever under an end load P is thought to depend on P, the length L, Young's modulus E and the second moment of area I.
(a) Write down the dimensions of each variable. Show that the dimensional matrix has rank 2, and hence find the number of dimensionless groups. Give a suitable set. [6]
(b) Beam theory shows that E and I appear only as the product EI. Use this, together with linearity, to reduce the result to δ = C PL³/(EI). Describe how you would confirm this experimentally and find C. [7]
(c) A steel cantilever (E = 210 GPa) of length 4 m is to be modelled at 1:10 scale using a geometrically similar aluminium model (E = 70 GPa). What model load corresponds to a full-scale load P, and how should model deflections be scaled? If the model deflects 2 mm, what is the full-scale deflection? [7]
markScheme: (a) δ [L], P [M L T⁻²], L [L], E [M L⁻¹ T⁻²], I [L⁴]
(a) M and T appear only as M T⁻² in P and E, so the rank is 2 (not 3); 5 − 2 = 3 groups
(a) For example δ/L, P/(EL²), I/L⁴
(b) Only EI matters, so the groups combine into PL²/(EI): δ/L = φ(PL²/EI)
(b) Linearity δ ∝ P gives δ = C PL³/(EI)
(b) Experiment: vary P, L and the section; plot δ against PL³/(EI) for all beams; a straight line through the origin with gradient C (expected 1/3)
(c) Similarity: P/(EL²) equal, so P_m = P_p(E_m/E_p)(L_m/L_p)² = P_p/300
(c) δ/L equal, so δ_p = 10δ_m = 20 mm
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) δ: L. P: M L T⁻². L: L. E: M L⁻¹ T⁻². I: L⁴. The exponents of M and T are (1, −2) for P and (1, −2) for E, and zero for the others. So the M and T rows of the dimensional matrix are proportional (T row = −2 × M row) and only two rows are independent. The rank is 2, not 3. By the Pi theorem there are 5 − 2 = 3 groups. A suitable set is Π₁ = δ/L, Π₂ = P/(EL²) and Π₃ = I/L⁴, so δ/L = φ(P/(EL²), I/L⁴). If you wrongly took k = 3, you would find only 2 groups and miss one.

(b) If E and I appear only as EI, the two independent groups must combine into one containing EI: Π₂/Π₃ = PL²/(EI). So δ/L = φ(PL²/EI). For a linear elastic beam with small deflections, doubling P doubles δ, so φ must be linear: δ/L = C × PL²/(EI), giving δ = C PL³/(EI). To test this, load several cantilevers of different lengths and cross-sections (and, if possible, materials) with a range of loads, measuring δ each time. Compute EI from the section dimensions and the material. Plot δ against PL³/(EI) for all the data. The points should lie on a single straight line through the origin, whose gradient is C. Beam theory predicts C = 1/3. Departures at large loads would show non-linearity (yield or large deflections). Scatter between beams would suggest an effect not included, such as end fixity.

(c) For similarity, the model must match P/(EL²) (and the geometry, so I/L⁴ matches automatically). So P_m = P_p × (E_m/E_p) × (L_m/L_p)² = P_p × (70/210) × (1/10)² = P_p/300. Deflections scale with length because δ/L is the same: δ_p = δ_m × (L_p/L_m) = 10δ_m. A model deflection of 2 mm therefore corresponds to 20 mm at full scale (on a 4 m beam, which is consistent with small-deflection theory). Self-weight has been ignored. If it mattered, the group ρgL/E would also have to match, which a small aluminium model cannot achieve with the same load scaling.
